newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU warns Israel over "excessive" clampdown. [CORRECTED 15:34 GMT]
newsitem.headline: EU warns Israel over "excessive" clampdown. [CORRECTED 15:34 GMT]

text.p: The European Union, which has a key mediating role in the Middle East peace process, said on Friday it was concerned about what it termed counter-productive measures introduced by Israel after last month's Jerusalem bombings.
Luxembourg Foreign Minister (corrects title) Jacques Poos, whose country currently holds the rotating EU presidency, said the 15-nation bloc would express its concerns to the Israeli government.

"The EU has decided to ask its representatives in Tel Aviv to make a demarche to Foreign Minister (David) Levy to make our concern known," Poos said in a letter to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

The EU was last month instrumental in bringing together Arafat and Levy for talks in Brussels to try to revive the stalled peace process, but any progress there was wiped out by two Islamic militant suicide bombers who killed 13 other people in a Jerusalem market on July 30.
Arafat wrote to Poos last week asking him to intervene and put pressure on Tel Aviv to lift some of the measures introduced after the bombings.

Israel halted peace talks with the PLO in response to the bombings and sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, stopping trade, preventing Palestinians from getting to jobs in Israel and freezing financial transfers.
"The European Union fully shares your concern about the disastrous effect of the measures decided by the Israeli government...many of these...are new and seem to be excessive," Poos wrote.
He said the measures were punishing the Palestinian population, although its responsibility for the bombings had not been established.
"Their only effect will be to strengthen those who fight against the peace process," Poos said.

The EU's special Middle East envoy, Miguel Angel Moratinos, has previously raised the bloc's concerns with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, saying certain measures, such as Israel withholding tax revenues, were counter-productive.
"Israel cannot expect that the Palestinian Authority searches for terrorists in the territories under its control if it cannot pay its police," Poos wrote.

The bombings and the subsequent Israeli crackdown sparked a war of words between the two sides. Arafat slammed the blockade as a declaration of war and told Palestinians to "prepare for what will come".
That statement, and angry words from Netanyahu, drew a sharp rebuke from U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright who urged both sides to revive a spirit of partnership on the issue of peace.
U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross is due in the region on Saturday on a mediation mission which Washington has said will focus on Israeli insistence on enhanced security.
Poos said the EU remained committed to the peace process and was at the disposal of both parties to help assist them in resuming talks.
